docs.title: Augmented Software Engineering
docs.text:
Build software. Use AI. Understand what you build.

A part-time program at Holberton School Albania. Learn the tools, the fundamentals and the full web stack, then build a portfolio with an AI assistant at your side.

Start here View roadmap

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
The last stage is your portfolio: two tracks of work you can show to an employer.

  • AI-Augmented Builds

    Take a product from idea to MVP with an AI assistant: write the specification, design the architecture, mock up the UI, prototype the API and assemble the MVP.

    5 projects · 40 h

  • HBnB

    A rental-listing web application, modelled on Airbnb and built in four phases: UML design, business logic and API, authentication and database, and a web client.

    4 phases · 360 h

docs.title: How you will work
docs.text:
The Holberton way: you learn by building, with your peers, and you leave able to explain and present what you built.

  • Project-based learning

    You learn by doing. Every concept comes with a project that has to run, pass the checks and be pushed to GitHub.

  • Peer learning

    You learn with and from your cohort: pair programming, code reviews and explaining your solution to someone else.

  • AI as a pair, not a replacement

    You prompt, review and correct AI output. The assistant writes a draft; you are responsible for what gets merged.

  • Understand what you ship

    If you can't explain it, you don't commit it. Reading and debugging code matter as much as writing it.

  • Soft skills

    Communication, teamwork, giving and receiving feedback, and presenting your work clearly to technical and non-technical people.

  • Work like a professional

    Git, pull requests, deadlines and code review from day one, and mock interviews to prepare for the real thing.

docs.title: AI Assistant
docs.text:
40 min Tools Needs: VS Code connected to WSL, a GitHub account

You will use three assistants in this program, and each has a different job. This tutorial sets them up and shows you how to use them without letting them do your learning for you.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Professional developers use AI every day: to explain unfamiliar code, draft boilerplate, find bugs and write tests. You will too, from the first week.

AI can produce something that looks right very quickly. What it cannot do is check its own assumptions, know what your project actually needs, or take responsibility for the result. That part is yours. A project that passes the Checker but that you cannot explain will not survive a peer review, and it will not survive a job interview either.

docs.title: Three assistants, three jobs
docs.text:
The three assistants and when to use each GitHub Copilot lives in VS Code and helps while you write code, with suggestions and chat about your open files. Claude or ChatGPT live in the browser and help when you need to understand something, explaining concepts and errors and comparing approaches. Clippy lives on the intranet and helps when you are stuck on a task, guiding your reasoning step by step without giving you code. IN VS CODE GitHub Copilot Suggestions as you type, chat about your open files while you write code IN THE BROWSER Claude or ChatGPT Explains concepts and errors, compares approaches when you need to understand ON THE INTRANET Clippy Guides your reasoning step by step, never gives code when you are stuck on a task

Copilot sees the files you have open, so it is the fastest way to ask about your code. Claude or ChatGPT have more room for a conversation, so they are better for understanding a concept or an error properly. Clippy knows Holberton's projects and is built to make you think: it asks questions and gives you the next step, not the answer.

docs.title: How to use any of them
docs.text:
Whichever assistant you open, the same loop applies.

The verify loop Ask with context, read the draft, test it yourself, and only then commit, and only what you can explain. If the test fails or you cannot explain it, go back and revise your question. Ask with context Read every line of the draft Test run it yourself Commit if you can explain it fails, or you cannot explain it: revise

The step people skip is Read. If you cannot say what a line does, you are not ready to test it, and you are certainly not ready to commit it.

docs.title: Step 1: Switch on GitHub Copilot in VS Code
docs.text:
Copilot is built into VS Code. You only need to sign in.

  1. Open VS Code connected to WSL, so the bottom left says WSL: Ubuntu.
  2. Hover over the Copilot icon in the status bar and choose Use AI Features.
  3. Sign in with your GitHub account and approve the request in the browser.

If your account has no Copilot plan, it is enrolled in Copilot Free automatically, which gives you a monthly allowance of suggestions and chat. If you are a student, you can also apply through GitHub Education for the free student plan. Plans and limits change often, so check the current details there.

Two shortcuts to learn now:

Keys What it opens Ctrl+Alt+I Chat view: a conversation about your project Ctrl+I Inline chat: ask about, or change, the selected code

Consider turning off inline suggestions while you learn the basics

Grey suggestions that appear as you type are useful once you know the language. In your first weeks they type the answer before you have thought of it, and you learn the syntax much more slowly. Hover over the Copilot icon in the status bar to switch code completions off. Chat keeps working, so you can still ask questions.

docs.title: Step 2: Set up a browser assistant
docs.text:
Create a free account on Claude or ChatGPT. One is enough; pick whichever you prefer. Keep it pinned in your browser next to the intranet.

Use it for the bigger questions:

  • Explain a concept from your project in plain language.
  • Read an error message with you and say what it means.
  • Compare two ways of solving something and their trade-offs.

docs.title: Step 3: Meet Clippy
docs.text:
Clippy lives on the intranet, on your project pages. It knows what each task asks for and is built to coach you rather than solve it.

Tell Clippy what you are trying to do, what you have tried and where you are stuck. It answers with questions and the next step of reasoning, not with code. That is deliberate. Use it when you are stuck on how to think about a task, before you go looking for code anywhere else.

docs.title: Ask well
docs.text:
A vague question gets a vague answer. A good prompt gives the assistant four things: what you are working on, what you tried, what happened, and what kind of help you want.

Explain an error

I'm writing a Python script on Ubuntu for a beginner project.
Running `python3 0-add.py` gives this error:

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

Explain what the error means and where to look in my code.
Don't rewrite the code for me.

Ask for a hint, not the answer

My task: write a function that returns the largest number in a list
without using max(). I tried looping over the list, but I don't know
what to compare each number against. Give me a hint for the next
step, not the solution.

Review code you wrote

Here is my solution to a task. It passes, but review it like a
senior developer: is anything unclear, fragile or unnecessary?
Explain each point. Don't give me a rewritten version.

[paste your code]

Notice the last line of each prompt. Saying what you do not want is the easiest way to keep the learning on your side.

docs.title: Rules for Holberton projects
docs.text:
• Do

    • Ask it to explain concepts, docs and error messages
    • Ask for a hint when you are stuck
    • Ask it to review code you wrote yourself
    • Ask it for test cases you had not thought of
    • Check what it says against the docs or by running it

  • Don't

    • Paste a task and submit whatever comes back
    • Commit a line you cannot explain
    • Paste passwords, tokens or .env files into any assistant
    • Paste a classmate's code without asking them
    • Trust a confident answer you have not tested

Your peers and mentors will ask you to explain your code. "The AI wrote it" is not an explanation.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
There is no Copilot icon in the status bar

Update VS Code with Help > Check for Updates, then restart it. If the icon is still missing, press Ctrl+Shift+P and run Chat: Open Chat, which also offers the sign-in.

Copilot says I have reached my limit

The free plan has a monthly allowance. Use the browser assistant or Clippy until it resets, or apply for the student plan through GitHub Education.

The answer looks right but the code fails

That happens often. Assistants guess at versions, file names and what your task requires. Paste the exact error back and say what you expected, or read the docs for the function it used.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. The Copilot icon in the status bar shows you are signed in.
  2. Open hello.py, select the print line, press Ctrl+I and ask explain this line. Read the answer.
  3. In Claude or ChatGPT, ask: What is the difference between running python3 hello.py and ./hello.py on Linux? Then try both in your terminal and see whether the answer was right.
  4. Open any project on the intranet and ask Clippy how to start the first task. Notice that it asks you questions back.

docs.text: Assistant Where Use it for Open it with GitHub Copilot VS Code Questions about your open code Ctrl+Alt+I, Ctrl+I Claude or ChatGPT Browser Concepts, errors, comparing approaches claude.ai, chatgpt.com Clippy Intranet project pages Reasoning through a task On the project page

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
30 min Tools Needs: WSL set up

VS Code is the editor you will use for every project in this program: Python, SQL, HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It installs on Windows and works inside Ubuntu, so you get a familiar window and a Linux machine underneath it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: A good editor does a lot of quiet work. It catches typos before the Checker does, keeps your formatting consistent, and puts a terminal, Git and an AI assistant in the same window as your code. Set it up properly once and you stop thinking about it.

docs.title: The window at a glance
docs.text:
The five parts of the VS Code window 1, the activity bar down the far left. 2, the side bar with the file explorer. 3, the editor in the middle, where you write code. 4, the panel at the bottom with the terminal. 5, the status bar along the bottom edge, whose left corner shows WSL: Ubuntu when VS Code is connected to Linux. EXPLORER ▾ holberton hello.py README.md 1 print("Hello, Holberton") 2 TERMINAL you@laptop:~/holberton$ python3 hello.py Hello, Holberton WSL: Ubuntu main Ln 1, Col 1 Python 1 2 3 4 5
  1. Activity bar. Switches the side bar between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions and Copilot Chat.
  2. Side bar. Shows whatever the activity bar picked. Most of the time, the files in your project.
  3. Editor. Where you write code. You can split it to see two files at once.
  4. Panel. The terminal lives here. It is a real Ubuntu terminal, the same one you used in the WSL tutorial.
  5. Status bar. The bottom left corner must say WSL: Ubuntu. That label tells you your code runs on Linux. Check it whenever something behaves strangely.

docs.title: Step 1: Install VS Code on Windows
docs.text:
Download it from code.visualstudio.com and run the installer. Tick these boxes when offered:

  • Add "Open with Code" action to the file context menu
  • Add "Open with Code" action to the directory context menu
  • Add to PATH

The last one lets you type code . in a terminal to open the current folder. You will use it constantly.

Install VS Code on Windows only. Do not install it inside Ubuntu.

docs.title: Step 2: Install the WSL extension
docs.text:
1. Open VS Code and press Ctrl+Shift+X to open Extensions.
  2. Search for WSL, published by Microsoft, and click Install.

docs.title: Step 3: Open your projects folder from Ubuntu
docs.text:
Open the Ubuntu terminal and run:

cd ~/holberton
code .

The first time, Ubuntu downloads a small helper called the VS Code Server. Give it a minute. A VS Code window opens with your holberton folder in the Explorer.

Look at the bottom left corner. It should say WSL: Ubuntu. Open the terminal with Ctrl+` (the key above Tab). The prompt looks like this:

yourname@LAPTOP:~/holberton$

That is Linux. Everything you type there runs on Ubuntu.

docs.title: Step 4: Install extensions on the Linux side
docs.text:
Extensions install separately on each side. Having one on Windows does not mean it works in the WSL window.

Open Extensions with Ctrl+Shift+X in the WSL window and install these. Each one shows an Install in WSL: Ubuntu button.

Extension Publisher What it gives you Python Microsoft Highlighting, error hints and the Python interpreter ESLint Microsoft Flags JavaScript mistakes as you type

Later modules add a few more. Keep the list short: every extension slows the editor down a little.

docs.title: Step 5: Settings that keep the Checker happy
docs.text:
Holberton's style checkers reject lines longer than 79 characters, spaces at the end of a line, and files without a final newline. VS Code can handle all three for you.

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON), and add these lines inside the curly braces:

{
  "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
  "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "editor.rulers": [79],
  "editor.renderWhitespace": "trailing",
  "[python]": { "editor.tabSize": 4 },
  "[javascript]": { "editor.tabSize": 2 }
}

If the file already has settings, add the new lines among them and separate each line with a comma. Save with Ctrl+S.

The ruler draws a thin line at column 79. Keep your code to the left of it.

docs.title: Step 6: Run your first file
docs.text:
In the Explorer, click the new-file icon and create hello.py:

print("Hello, Holberton")

Run it in the terminal:

python3 hello.py

The output appears right below. The Checker runs your files from a terminal exactly like this, so get used to running them the same way rather than with a Run button.

AI in the loop

VS Code has GitHub Copilot built in. You switch it on in the next tutorial, together with a browser assistant and Clippy, and learn when to use which.

docs.title: Shortcuts worth knowing
docs.text: Keys What it does Ctrl+Shift+P Command palette. Everything VS Code can do is in here Ctrl+P Jump to a file by typing part of its name Ctrl+` Show or hide the terminal Ctrl+B Show or hide the side bar Ctrl+Shift+E File explorer Ctrl+/ Comment or uncomment the selected lines Alt+Up / Alt+Down Move the current line up or down Ctrl+D Select the next match of the selected word

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
code: command not found in Ubuntu

Close and reopen the Ubuntu terminal. If it still fails, reinstall VS Code on Windows and make sure Add to PATH is ticked, then restart the laptop.

The status bar does not say WSL: Ubuntu

You opened the folder from Windows. Close the window, open the Ubuntu terminal, and run cd ~/holberton && code . again.

An extension is installed but does nothing

It is installed on the Windows side only. Open Extensions in the WSL window and click Install in WSL: Ubuntu.

Everything is slow, and Git takes seconds

Your project is under /mnt/c. Move it into ~/holberton, as in the WSL tutorial.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. The bottom left corner says WSL: Ubuntu.
  2. In the VS Code terminal, pwd prints /home/yourname/holberton.
  3. python3 hello.py prints Hello, Holberton.
  4. Type a line longer than the ruler in hello.py. You can see where it crosses column 79.
  5. Add a few spaces at the end of a line and save. They disappear.

docs.title: WSL
docs.text:
35 min Tools Needs: Windows 10 (2004+) or 11, admin rights

WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, runs a real Ubuntu inside Windows. Every project in this program is written, run and checked on Linux, so this is where your code will live.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Almost every server, cloud machine and container you will deploy to runs Linux. Holberton projects are tested on Ubuntu too, so code that works on Windows can still fail the Checker because of a path, a line ending or a missing command.

WSL removes that gap. You keep the Windows you are used to for your browser, Slack and VS Code. Your code runs on Linux, and the two share files. This setup is required for the program.

On a Mac or Linux?

You do not need WSL. macOS and Linux already have a Unix terminal. Go straight to VS Code and use your normal terminal wherever these tutorials say Ubuntu terminal.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
Windows and Ubuntu side by side with WSL On the Windows side you have your apps, such as VS Code and the browser, and your Windows files. On the Ubuntu side, inside WSL, your code runs with Python, Node.js and Git, and your projects live in a folder in your Linux home. VS Code connects to Ubuntu through the WSL extension. Windows files are reachable from Ubuntu under slash mnt slash c. WINDOWS VS Code, browser, Slack what you look at and type in Your Windows files C:\Users\you\Documents UBUNTU, INSIDE WSL Python, Node.js, Git where the code actually runs Your projects ~/holberton WSL extension /mnt/c

One thing to hold on to: the window is Windows, the code is Linux.

docs.title: Step 1: Check your Windows
docs.text:
Press Win+R, type winver and press Enter. You need Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or later. If you are on an older version, run Windows Update first.

Then open Task Manager with Ctrl+Shift+Esc, go to Performance, then CPU, and find the line Virtualization. It should say Enabled. If it says disabled, see When something goes wrong before you continue.

docs.title: Step 2: Install WSL
docs.text:
Right-click the Start button and choose Terminal (Admin). On Windows 10 this may be called Windows PowerShell (Admin). Then run:

wsl --install

This turns on the Windows features WSL needs, downloads the Linux kernel and installs Ubuntu. It takes a few minutes. Restart when it asks.

docs.title: Step 3: Create your Linux user
docs.text:
After the restart, Ubuntu opens by itself and asks for a username and a password.

  • Username: lowercase, no spaces. It does not have to match your Windows name.
  • Password: pick one you will remember. You type it every time you run a command with sudo.

Linux shows nothing while you type a password, not even dots. That is normal. Type it and press Enter.

Check it worked. Back in the Windows terminal, run:

wsl --list --verbose

You want to see Ubuntu with version 2:

  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2

docs.title: Step 4: Update Ubuntu and install the basics
docs.text:
Open Ubuntu from the Start menu. Everything from here on runs in the Ubuntu terminal, not in PowerShell.

Update the package lists and upgrade what is installed:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

Then install the tools the first projects need:

sudo apt install -y build-essential git curl python3 python3-pip python3-venv

Check them:

python3 --version
git --version

You should see Python 3.10 or later, and any recent Git version.

AI in the loop

When an install fails, copy the full error message into Claude or ChatGPT and ask what it means and what each suggested fix does. Run a fix only once you understand what it changes. Pasting commands you do not understand into a terminal with sudo is how people break their setup.

docs.title: Step 5: Make your projects folder
docs.text:
This is the one WSL rule worth memorising.

Keep your projects in your Linux home folder. Files there live on the Linux filesystem and are fast. Files under /mnt/c live on the Windows filesystem, and every read crosses a bridge. Git and Python become noticeably slow, and file permissions behave strangely.

mkdir -p ~/holberton
cd ~/holberton
pwd

You should see /home/yourname/holberton. That is where every project in this program goes.

To look at the folder in Windows Explorer, run:

explorer.exe .

The dot means this folder. Explorer opens it under Linux in the sidebar.

Make Ubuntu your default terminal

In Windows Terminal, open Settings, set Default profile to Ubuntu and save. Every new terminal tab then opens straight into Linux.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
wsl --install fails, or Virtualization says disabled

Virtualisation is turned off in your BIOS. Restart, enter the BIOS setup (usually F2, F10 or Del while the laptop starts), and enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V, sometimes called SVM. Save, restart and run wsl --install again.

wsl --list --verbose shows version 1

Run wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2 in PowerShell and wait. It can take a few minutes. Then run wsl --set-default-version 2 so future installs use version 2.

Ubuntu opens and closes straight away

Run wsl --update in PowerShell, restart the laptop and open Ubuntu again.

I forgot my Linux password

In PowerShell, run wsl -u root to open Ubuntu as the administrator account. Then run passwd yourname, set a new password, and type exit.

Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock

Another update is running in the background. Wait a minute and run your apt command again.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
1. In PowerShell, wsl --list --verbose shows Ubuntu with version 2.
  2. In the Ubuntu terminal, cd ~/holberton && pwd prints /home/yourname/holberton, not a /mnt/c path.
  3. python3 --version prints 3.10 or later.
  4. git --version prints a version number.
  5. explorer.exe . opens your holberton folder in Windows Explorer.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Command Where What it does wsl --install PowerShell (Admin) Installs WSL and Ubuntu wsl --list --verbose PowerShell Shows installed Linux versions wsl --update PowerShell Updates WSL itself sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y Ubuntu Updates Ubuntu's packages sudo apt install -y name Ubuntu Installs a package cd ~/holberton Ubuntu Goes to your projects folder explorer.exe . Ubuntu Opens the current folder in Windows Explorer

docs.title: Zero Day
docs.text:
30 min Tools Needs: the email Holberton sent you

Before you write any code, you need your accounts working and you need to know how learning works here. This page covers both. Do it before your first day, not during it.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Holberton works differently from a classroom. Nobody lectures you through the material, and nobody hands you the answer. If you start expecting that, the first weeks feel confusing. If you know the method, they feel fast.

The accounts matter for a plainer reason: they are how your work gets seen and checked. A broken login in week one turns into a missing submission in week two.

docs.title: How learning works at Holberton
docs.text:
You learn by building. Every concept arrives as a project with a deadline, and you work out how to solve it with your peers, the documentation and your AI tools. The project is the lesson.

The Holberton learning loop Four steps repeat for every project. Build: you write the code yourself. Check: the Checker tests it instantly. Review: peers read and question it. Explain: you justify every decision. Then the next project starts the loop again. 1 Build you write the code 2 Check the Checker tests it 3 Review peers question it 4 Explain you justify it next project

Build. You write the solution yourself. Searching, reading docs and asking for help are all part of the work; copying a finished answer is not.

Check. The Checker runs your code against the project's tests and tells you straight away what passes and what fails. Fix, push, check again.

Review. Your peers read your code and ask why it works the way it does. You do the same for them, and you learn as much from reading their solutions as from writing yours.

Explain. You should be able to justify every line you submit. That is the skill employers test in interviews, and it is the skill AI makes more valuable, not less.

docs.title: Your week
docs.text:
• Work every day

    A little every day beats a long weekend session. Projects have deadlines and build on each other, so falling behind compounds.

  • Peer learning days

    You work through problems with your cohort, review each other's code and explain your solutions out loud.

  • Mentor days

    Time with mentors to unblock hard problems, get feedback on your approach and prepare for interviews.

AI in the loop

AI is a collaborator here, not a shortcut. It drafts quickly, but it cannot check its own assumptions or take responsibility for the result. You can, and that is the job. On the intranet you also have Clippy, Holberton's own assistant. It helps you reason through a task step by step instead of giving you the code. You set up all of your assistants in the AI Assistant tutorial.

docs.title: The platforms
docs.text:
The platforms you need The intranet for projects, the Checker and Clippy. Slack for communication, with the same login as the intranet. GitHub for your code and portfolio, on your own separate account. Your laptop, running Ubuntu inside WSL, which you set up in the next tutorial. Intranet Projects, the Checker, Clippy, your scores intranet.hbtn.io Slack Questions, announcements, your cohort same login as the intranet GitHub Your code, and your public portfolio your own separate account Your laptop Ubuntu inside WSL, where your code runs next tutorial

The intranet and Slack share one login. GitHub is your own account, and it is the one that follows you after you finish the program.

docs.title: Step 1: Set up the intranet
docs.text:
Go to intranet.hbtn.io and log in with the credentials from your welcome email. Bookmark the page. You will open it every day.

Then finish your profile:

  1. Click your profile icon in the bottom left corner.
  2. Fill in every field marked with an asterisk.
  3. Add a photo. A plain head and shoulders shot is fine. This is the photo your mentors and future employers will see.
  4. Save.

Do not change your password yet

Slack reads your account from the intranet. Change the password now and you may lock yourself out of Slack before it has synced. Wait until everything on this page works.

docs.title: Step 2: Join Slack
docs.text:
Open the intranet and find the Slack link in the left navigation panel. Log in with the same credentials.

You are added to your cohort channel automatically. Install the desktop or phone app as well. The browser tab is easy to forget, and Slack is where schedule changes get announced.

docs.title: Step 3: Create your GitHub account
docs.text:
Already have one you use professionally? Use it and skip to Step 4.

Otherwise go to github.com/signup. Two choices matter here.

The email. Use one you will still read in five years. Not a work or school address that gets shut off when you leave.

The username. It becomes part of your professional identity and appears in every project link you send to an employer. Something close to your real name works well. Something you thought was funny at nineteen does not.

When you have it, go back to your intranet profile and add the username there. The Checker uses it to find your repositories, so a typo means your projects do not get checked.

docs.title: Step 4: Get your laptop ready
docs.text:
You write and run all your code on your own laptop, inside Ubuntu Linux. On Windows that means WSL, which is required for this program. You set it up in the next tutorial. Before then, check two things:

  • You can install software on the laptop. You need administrator rights.
  • Windows is up to date: Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or later.

On a Mac or Linux?

You already have a Unix terminal. Skip the WSL tutorial and go straight to VS Code.

docs.title: Check yourself
docs.text:
Five minutes, and it proves everything works.

  1. Log in to the intranet and confirm your profile shows your photo and your GitHub username.
  2. Post a short hello in your cohort channel on Slack.
  3. Open your GitHub profile page and check the username reads the way you want an employer to read it.
  4. Open any project on the intranet and find Clippy.

If any of these fails, ask in Slack now. That is exactly what the channel is for.
